title: Φόνοι ἡγεμόνων
titleEn: The Leaders’ Kills and the Flight over the Ditch — Iliad 16.306–393
part: The Leaders’ Kills and the Flight over the Ditch (16.306–393)
about: The Danaan leaders each kill a man as the Trojan battle breaks into single fights. Patroclus wounds Areilycus and Menelaus Thoas; Meges, Antilochus and Thrasymedes strike down Amphiclus, Atymnius and Maris, the sons of Amisodarus who raised the Chimaera; the lesser Ajax takes Cleobulus alive and kills him; Peneleos beheads Lycon, and Meriones and Idomeneus kill Acamas and Erymas. The Danaans fall on the Trojans like wolves on strayed lambs, and the Trojans forget their courage. Only the great Ajax is still trying to cast at Hector, who shelters behind his shield and, seeing the day turn, holds his ground a while to save his companions. Then the rout comes like a cloud from Olympus. Hector’s horses carry him off, the Trojan army is trapped behind the dug ditch, and many chariots are left broken in it. Patroclus presses on, driving men from their chariots, and Achilles’ deathless horses leap the ditch in pursuit of Hector, who escapes. The poet likens the Trojan mares groaning as they run to rivers swollen by Zeus’s storm in punishment of crooked judges.

sentences.t:
ἔνθα δ’ ἀνὴρ ἕλεν ἄνδρα κεδασθείσης ὑσμίνης
ἡγεμόνων.
sentences.l:
Then a man took a man, the battle having been scattered
of the leaders.
sentences.i: Then, with the battle scattered, one of the leaders killed a man.
sentences.n: A run of single kills by the leaders begins here, each man for a man; line 351 sums it up as ‘these leaders of the Danaans took a man each’. ἡγεμόνων ‘of the leaders’ is the last word of the unit and goes with ἀνήρ, ‘a man of the leaders’, not with the battle. κεδασθείσης ὑσμίνης is a genitive absolute, ‘the battle having been scattered’ (aorist passive participle of κεδάννυμι ‘scatter’), meaning the line has broken up into separate fights. ἕλεν is the aorist of αἱρέω ‘take’, and ‘took’ for ‘killed’ is how the poet says it. This line, without ἡγεμόνων, stands also at 15.328. A new paragraph begins here.

sentences.t:
πρῶτος δὲ Μενοιτίου ἄλκιμος υἱὸς
αὐτίκ’ ἄρα στρεφθέντος Ἀρηϊλύκου βάλε μηρὸν
ἔγχεϊ ὀξυόεντι, διὰ πρὸ δὲ χαλκὸν ἔλασσε·
sentences.i: The first was Menoetius’ sturdy son: the moment Areilycus turned, he struck him in the thigh with his sharp spear and drove the bronze clean through;
sentences.n: Menoetius’ sturdy son is Patroclus, whom the poet does not name until line 372; ἄλκιμος ‘sturdy’ is his stock epithet in this formula. στρεφθέντος Ἀρηϊλύκου is a genitive absolute, ‘Areilycus having turned’ and so the thrust finds him in the thigh. ἔγχεϊ ὀξυόεντι is ‘with a sharp spear’, the dative of the instrument. διὰ πρὸ δὲ … ἔλασσε is a verb split from its prefixes, ‘drove the bronze clean through’; ἔλασσε is the aorist of ἐλαύνω ‘drive’, and χαλκόν ‘bronze’ here means the spearhead.

sentences.t:
ῥῆξεν δ’ ὀστέον ἔγχος, ὃ δὲ πρηνὴς ἐπὶ γαίῃ
κάππεσ’·
sentences.l:
and the spear broke the bone, and he headlong upon the earth
fell down;
sentences.i: The spear broke the bone, and he fell face down on the earth;
sentences.n: ὃ δέ ‘and he’ is Areilycus again. ῥῆξεν is the aorist of ῥήγνυμι ‘break’ with ἔγχος ‘spear’ as its subject. πρηνής is ‘headlong, face forward’, and the plain English says ‘face down’ of a man. κάππεσ’ is κατέπεσε, with the τ of κατ- taken over by the π of πεσ- and the final ε dropped before the next word; it is one word, ‘fell down’.

sentences.t:
ἀτὰρ Μενέλαος ἀρήϊος οὖτα Θόαντα
στέρνον γυμνωθέντα παρ’ ἀσπίδα, λῦσε δὲ γυῖα.
sentences.l:
but warlike Menelaus wounded Thoas
in the chest, laid bare beside the shield, and loosed his limbs.
sentences.i: And warlike Menelaus wounded Thoas, whose chest had been bared beside his shield, and loosed his limbs.
sentences.n: ἀτάρ ‘but, and’ starts a new kill. ἀρήϊος ‘warlike’ is the stock epithet of Menelaus. οὖτα is the aorist of οὐτάω ‘wound’. γυμνωθέντα is the aorist passive participle of γυμνόω ‘lay bare’, agreeing with Θόαντα, and στέρνον ‘in the chest’ is the part struck, the accusative of the place wounded; παρ’ ἀσπίδα ‘beside the shield’ says where the chest lay bare, and the Greek does not say how it came to be uncovered. λῦσε δὲ γυῖα ‘and loosed his limbs’ is the idiom for killing, here as at 4.469.

sentences.t:
Φυλεΐδης δ’ Ἄμφικλον ἐφορμηθέντα δοκεύσας
ἔφθη ὀρεξάμενος πρυμνὸν σκέλος, ἔνθα πάχιστος
μυὼν ἀνθρώπου πέλεται·
sentences.i: The son of Phyleus watched Amphiclus rush at him and got in first, thrusting at the leg at its root, where a man’s muscle is thickest;
sentences.n: Φυλεΐδης ‘son of Phyleus’ is Meges, who is not named in these lines (Μέγης … Φυλεΐδης stand together at 2.627–628, and the patronymic alone is used of him at 5.72); the patronymic takes the hyphen in the literal line. ἐφορμηθέντα is the aorist passive participle of ἐφορμάομαι ‘rush at’, agreeing with Ἄμφικλον, and δοκεύσας ‘having watched for’ comes from δοκεύω ‘watch, lie in wait for’. ἔφθη ὀρεξάμενος is ‘got in first, reaching out’: ἔφθη is the aorist of φθάνω ‘be first’ and ὀρεξάμενος the aorist middle participle of ὀρέγω ‘reach’. The weapon is not named, but the next line has the spear’s point. πρυμνόν ‘at its root’ is the base of the leg, and πάχιστος ‘thickest’ is the superlative of παχύς.

sentences.t:
περὶ δ’ ἔγχεος αἰχμῇ
νεῦρα διεσχίσθη· τὸν δὲ σκότος ὄσσε κάλυψε.
sentences.l:
and about the point of the spear
the sinews were torn apart; and darkness covered his two eyes.
sentences.i: and the sinews were torn apart around the spear’s point; and darkness covered his eyes.
sentences.n: περὶ … αἰχμῇ is ‘about the point’, with αἰχμή ‘point’ in the dative and the preposition standing first in its clause. διεσχίσθη is the aorist passive of διασχίζω ‘split apart’, and νεῦρα ‘sinews’ is the plural subject taken with a singular verb, as often with a neuter plural. τὸν δὲ σκότος ὄσσε κάλυψε is a half-line death formula, the second half of the line: τόν ‘him’ and ὄσσε ‘eyes’ are both accusative, whole and part, and ὄσσε is the dual, ‘his two eyes’ in the literal line.

sentences.t:
Νεστορίδαι δ’ ὃ μὲν οὔτασ’ Ἀτύμνιον ὀξέϊ δουρὶ
Ἀντίλοχος, λαπάρης δὲ διήλασε χάλκεον ἔγχος·
sentences.l:
And Nestor’s-sons, the one wounded Atymnius with sharp spear,
Antilochus, and through the flank drove the bronze spear;
sentences.i: Of the sons of Nestor, Antilochus wounded Atymnius with his sharp spear and drove the bronze spear through his flank;
sentences.n: Νεστορίδαι is the plural patronymic, ‘sons of Nestor’, here Antilochus and Thrasymedes. ὃ μέν ‘the one’ is Antilochus, named at the start of the next line; the other son, Thrasymedes, comes in at 321. οὔτασ’ is οὔτασε, the aorist of οὐτάω ‘wound’. ὀξέϊ δουρί is ‘with a sharp spear’, the dative of δόρυ. λαπάρης is ‘the flank’, the genitive with διήλασε ‘drove through’, and χάλκεον ἔγχος is ‘the bronze spear’.

sentences.t: ἤριπε δὲ προπάροιθε.
sentences.l: and he crashed down in front.
sentences.i: and he crashed down in front.
sentences.n: The subject is Atymnius. ἤριπε ‘crashed down’ is the aorist of ἐρείπω, a word for a big body falling. προπάροιθε is an adverb, ‘in front, forward’; the Greek does not say in front of whom.

sentences.t:
Μάρις δ’ αὐτοσχεδὰ δουρὶ
Ἀντιλόχῳ ἐπόρουσε κασιγνήτοιο χολωθεὶς
στὰς πρόσθεν νέκυος·
sentences.i: Maris, angry for his brother, took his stand in front of the corpse and rushed at Antilochus with his spear at close quarters;
sentences.n: Μάρις is the brother of the man just killed; κασιγνήτοιο ‘for his brother’ is the genitive of the cause of anger, and χολωθείς ‘angered’ is the aorist passive participle of χολόω (compare χόλος ‘anger’). The corpse in front of which he stands is Atymnius’. αὐτοσχεδά is the form of αὐτοσχεδόν ‘at close quarters’ with final -α. στάς is the aorist participle of ἵστημι, ‘having taken his stand’; ἐπόρουσε is the aorist of ἐπορούω ‘rush at’, with the dative Ἀντιλόχῳ.

sentences.t:
τοῦ δ’ ἀντίθεος Θρασυμήδης
ἔφθη ὀρεξάμενος πρὶν οὐτάσαι, οὐδ’ ἀφάμαρτεν,
ὦμον ἄφαρ·
sentences.i: but godlike Thrasymedes got in first, thrusting before Maris could wound him, and did not miss: he struck at once at the shoulder;
sentences.n: Thrasymedes is Antilochus’ brother, the other son of Nestor; ἀντίθεος ‘godlike’ is his stock epithet. τοῦ ‘him’ is Maris, the genitive after ἔφθη ‘got in first’, since φθάνω can take the genitive of the man outstripped (at 313 the same verb has no such object). πρὶν οὐτάσαι is ‘before he could wound’, with the infinitive after πρίν. οὐδ’ ἀφάμαρτεν is ‘and did not miss’, aorist of ἀφαμαρτάνω. ὦμον ‘the shoulder’ is the target, and ἄφαρ ‘at once’ qualifies the whole stroke; the weapon is the spear mentioned in the next line.

sentences.t:
πρυμνὸν δὲ βραχίονα δουρὸς ἀκωκὴ
δρύψ’ ἀπὸ μυώνων, ἀπὸ δ’ ὀστέον ἄχρις ἄραξε·
sentences.l:
and the upper arm at its root the tip of the spear
tore away from the muscles, and the bone it crushed right through;
sentences.i: and the tip of the spear tore his arm, at its root, away from the muscles and crushed the bone right through;
sentences.n: βραχίονα is ‘the upper arm’, with πρυμνόν ‘at its root’ saying where it was torn. δουρὸς ἀκωκή is ‘the tip of the spear’ (δόρυ, genitive δουρός); the word is ἀκωκή ‘point, tip’, kept apart from αἰχμή ‘point’ in line 315. δρύψ’ is δρύψε, the aorist of δρύπτω ‘tear’, and ἀπὸ μυώνων is ‘from the muscles’ (μυών, plural μυῶνες). ἀπὸ … ἄραξε has its preverb split off: ἄραξε is the aorist of ἀράσσω ‘crush’, and ἄχρις ‘right through’ is an adverb.

sentences.t: δούπησεν δὲ πεσών, κατὰ δὲ σκότος ὄσσε κάλυψεν.
sentences.l: and he fell with a thud, and down darkness covered his two eyes.
sentences.i: and he fell with a thud, and darkness covered his eyes.
sentences.n: The subject is Maris. δούπησεν is the aorist of δουπέω, ‘make a thud’, the noise of a heavy body falling (δοῦπος). κατά is a preverb parted from κάλυψεν; the second half of the line is the death formula of 316, with σκότος ‘darkness’ the subject and ὄσσε ‘two eyes’ its dual object.

sentences.t:
ὣς τὼ μὲν δοιοῖσι κασιγνήτοισι δαμέντε
βήτην εἰς Ἔρεβος Σαρπηδόνος ἐσθλοὶ ἑταῖροι
υἷες ἀκοντισταὶ Ἀμισωδάρου,
sentences.l:
So the two, by two brothers overcome,
went to Erebus, Sarpedon’s good companions,
sons, javelin-throwers, of Amisodarus,
sentences.i: So the two sons of Amisodarus, javelin-throwers and Sarpedon’s good companions, overcome by two brothers, went down to Erebus,
sentences.n: τώ and δαμέντε are duals: ‘the two’, ‘having been overcome’ (aorist passive participle of δαμάζω), and so is βήτην ‘went’. ὣς τὼ μέν ‘so the two’ looks back to Atymnius and Maris, who were themselves brothers; δοιοῖσι κασιγνήτοισι ‘by two brothers’ means Antilochus and Thrasymedes. Ἔρεβος is Erebus, the dark of the underworld, here simply where the dead go. Σαρπηδόνος ἐσθλοὶ ἑταῖροι is ‘Sarpedon’s good companions’, and υἷες ἀκοντισταί Ἀμισωδάρου ‘sons of Amisodarus, javelin-throwers’ names them (ἀκοντιστής ‘javelin-thrower’ is from ἀκοντίζω ‘cast’).

sentences.t:
ὅς ῥα Χίμαιραν
θρέψεν ἀμαιμακέτην πολέσιν κακὸν ἀνθρώποισιν.
sentences.l:
who indeed reared the Chimaera,
the huge one, an evil to many men.
sentences.i: He was the man who reared that huge creature, the Chimaera, an evil to many men.
sentences.n: This is the Chimaera of Bellerophon’s story (6.179), and ὅς ῥα ‘who indeed’ ties Amisodarus to it as to something known. θρέψεν is θρέψε, aorist of τρέφω ‘rear’. ἀμαιμακέτην is an adjective whose meaning is not known; the translation ‘huge’ follows the Odyssey’s use of the word for a mast and is a guess. πολέσιν is the epic dative plural of πολύς ‘many’, and κακὸν ἀνθρώποισιν is ‘an evil to men’.

sentences.t:
Αἴας δὲ Κλεόβουλον Ὀϊλιάδης ἐπορούσας
ζωὸν ἕλε βλαφθέντα κατὰ κλόνον·
sentences.l:
And Ajax, Oileus’-son, having rushed at Cleobulus,
took him alive, hindered in the turmoil;
sentences.i: Ajax, son of Oileus, rushed at Cleobulus, who was hindered in the turmoil, and took him alive;
sentences.n: Ὀϊλιάδης ‘son of Oileus’ is the lesser Ajax (Oileus’ Ajax, called ‘smaller’ at 2.527–528), so the poet can tell him from the great Ajax of line 358; the patronymic takes the hyphen in the literal line. ἐπορούσας is the aorist participle of ἐπορούω ‘rush at’. Κλεόβουλον is the object of ἕλε, ἐπορούσας standing without an object of its own; ζωὸν ἕλε is ‘took alive’, ἕλε being the aorist of αἱρέω, and βλαφθέντα, aorist passive participle of βλάπτω, means ‘hindered’; what hindered him is not said. κατὰ κλόνον is ‘in the turmoil’ of the fight.

sentences.t:
ἀλλά οἱ αὖθι
λῦσε μένος πλήξας ξίφει αὐχένα κωπήεντι.
sentences.l:
but there on the spot
he loosed his might, having struck him on the neck with a hilted sword.
sentences.i: but there and then Ajax loosed his might, striking him on the neck with a hilted sword.
sentences.n: ἀλλά ‘but’ answers the capture: the man is taken alive, but is killed on the spot. οἱ is ‘for him’ (dative of ἑ). λῦσε μένος ‘loosed his might’ is the same idiom as λῦσε γυῖα ‘loosed his limbs’ (312), a way of saying he killed him. αὖθι is ‘there, on the spot’. πλήξας is the aorist participle of πλήσσω ‘strike’, αὐχένα the neck, and ξίφει κωπήεντι ‘with a hilted sword’, with κωπήεις from κώπη ‘hilt’.

sentences.t: πᾶν δ’ ὑπεθερμάνθη ξίφος αἵματι·
sentences.l: and the whole sword grew warm beneath with blood;
sentences.i: and the whole sword grew warm with blood;
sentences.n: πᾶν ξίφος is ‘the whole sword’, the whole length of it wet with blood. ὑπεθερμάνθη is the aorist passive of ὑποθερμαίνω ‘warm’; the prefix ὑπο- is read as ‘gradually, from beneath’ and is left untranslated in the plain English (the literal line keeps ‘beneath’), and that reading is not certain.

sentences.t:
τὸν δὲ κατ’ ὄσσε
ἔλλαβε πορφύρεος θάνατος καὶ μοῖρα κραταιή.
sentences.l:
and him, down over the eyes,
seized purple death and strong fate.
sentences.i: and purple death and strong fate seized him, down over his eyes.
sentences.n: Cleobulus is the one seized. Line 334 stands also at 5.83. κατ’ ὄσσε is ‘down over the eyes’, κατά with the accusative of the part covered. πορφύρεος ‘purple’ is a dark colour, and the English keeps the colour word. ἔλλαβε is ‘seized’, the aorist of λαμβάνω with the accusative of the person; μοῖρα is ‘fate’ and κραταιή ‘strong’, an adjective related to κρατερός.

sentences.t: Πηνέλεως δὲ Λύκων τε συνέδραμον·
sentences.l: And Peneleos and Lycon ran together;
sentences.i: Peneleos and Lycon closed with one another;
sentences.n: Πηνέλεως is one of the Boeotian leaders (named first at 2.494); the English writes his name Peneleos. Λύκων is Lycon. The verb συνέδραμον (aorist of συντρέχω) is plural for the two names together, and ‘ran together’ means ‘met in combat’. The same verb closes the first sentence of line 337, for a second clash.

sentences.t:
ἔγχεσι μὲν γὰρ
ἤμβροτον ἀλλήλων, μέλεον δ’ ἠκόντισαν ἄμφω·
sentences.l:
for with spears they missed
one another, and idly they both cast;
sentences.i: for they missed one another with their spears, both casting to no purpose;
sentences.n: ἔγχεσι is the dative plural ‘with spears’. ἤμβροτον is the aorist of ἁμαρτάνω ‘miss’; it takes the genitive ἀλλήλων ‘of one another’. μέλεον is a neuter adjective used as an adverb, ‘to no purpose, idly’, and ἠκόντισαν is the aorist of ἀκοντίζω ‘cast’. ἄμφω ‘both’ is the subject’s second mention.

sentences.t: τὼ δ’ αὖτις ξιφέεσσι συνέδραμον.
sentences.l: and the two again with swords ran together.
sentences.i: and the two closed again, this time with swords.
sentences.n: τώ is the dual article, ‘the two’, and ξιφέεσσι is the epic dative plural of ξίφος ‘sword’. The spears have been cast and missed (336), so the fight goes on at close quarters.

sentences.t:
ἔνθα Λύκων μὲν
ἱπποκόμου κόρυθος φάλον ἤλασεν, ἀμφὶ δὲ καυλὸν
φάσγανον ἐρραίσθη·
sentences.i: Then Lycon struck the ridge of the helmet with its horsehair plume, and his sword was shattered near the hilt;
sentences.n: ἱπποκόμου κόρυθος is ‘of the horse-plumed helmet’ (κόρυς, genitive κόρυθος). φάλον is the helmet’s ridge, which is the usual explanation of the word; its sense is not certain. ἤλασεν is the aorist of ἐλαύνω ‘drive’, here a sword-stroke, with the sword unnamed. ἀμφὶ δὲ καυλόν … ἐρραίσθη is ‘about the stem … was shattered’: ἐρραίσθη is the aorist passive of ῥαίω ‘shatter’, and φάσγανον is another word for ‘sword’ (ξίφος is the usual one). καυλός is literally ‘stem’; on a sword it is understood as the part by the hilt, which the plain English says and the Greek does not; the exact part is not certain, and the table’s ‘socket’ (a spear’s καυλός) does not fit a sword.

sentences.t:
ὃ δ’ ὑπ’ οὔατος αὐχένα θεῖνε
Πηνέλεως, πᾶν δ’ εἴσω ἔδυ ξίφος, ἔσχεθε δ’ οἶον
δέρμα,
sentences.l:
and he, beneath the ear, the neck struck,
Peneleos, and the whole sword went within, and alone
the skin held,
sentences.i: Peneleos struck him on the neck beneath the ear, and the whole sword went in, and only the skin held,
sentences.n: ὃ δέ ‘and he’ is Peneleos, the man named in the line. θεῖνε is ἔθεινε, the imperfect without the augment, of θείνω ‘strike’. ὑπ’ οὔατος is ‘beneath the ear’. πᾶν … ξίφος is ‘the whole sword’, and εἴσω ‘within’ is an adverb. ἔσχεθε is ‘held’, with οἶον ‘alone’ agreeing with δέρμα ‘skin’: nothing but the skin kept the head on, as the next unit says. The sentence runs over the line-end into 341.

sentences.t: παρηέρθη δὲ κάρη, ὑπέλυντο δὲ γυῖα.
sentences.l: and the head was hung aside, and his limbs were loosed beneath him.
sentences.i: and the head hung over to one side, and his limbs were loosed beneath him.
sentences.n: παρηέρθη is the aorist passive of παραείρω, ‘lift to the side, let hang to one side’, so the head hangs from the strip of skin. ὑπέλυντο is the aorist middle-passive (the form without -θη-) of ὑπολύω ‘loose from beneath’, with γυῖα ‘limbs’ the subject, the same death idiom as ‘loosed his limbs’ (312) turned into the passive.

sentences.t:
Μηριόνης δ’ Ἀκάμαντα κιχεὶς ποσὶ καρπαλίμοισι
νύξ’ ἵππων ἐπιβησόμενον κατὰ δεξιὸν ὦμον·
sentences.l:
And Meriones, having overtaken Acamas with quick feet,
stabbed him, as he was about to mount the horses, in the right shoulder;
sentences.i: Meriones overtook Acamas on his quick feet and stabbed him in the right shoulder as he was about to mount his horses;
sentences.n: κιχεὶς is the aorist participle of κιχάνω ‘overtake’, and ποσὶ καρπαλίμοισι is ‘with quick feet’, the dative of the means; Meriones is on foot. νύξ’ is νύξε, the aorist of νύσσω ‘stab’. ἵππων ἐπιβησόμενον is ‘about to mount the horses’, the future participle of ἐπιβαίνω with the genitive; ‘the horses’ stand for the chariot he is stepping up to. Line 343 stands also at 5.46 with another man, and κατὰ δεξιὸν ὦμον is ‘in the right shoulder’.

sentences.t: ἤριπε δ’ ἐξ ὀχέων, κατὰ δ’ ὀφθαλμῶν κέχυτ’ ἀχλύς.
sentences.l: and he crashed down from the chariot, and down over his eyes was poured a haze.
sentences.i: and he crashed down from his chariot, and a haze was poured down over his eyes.
sentences.n: ἤριπε is ‘crashed down’ again (319). ὀχέων is the genitive plural of ὄχεα, a plural that stands for one chariot. κατὰ … κέχυτ’ is the verb split from its prefix: κέχυτο is the pluperfect passive of χέω ‘pour’, ‘had been poured’, put in the plain past in English. ἀχλύς is ‘haze’, the mist of dying that comes over the eyes, as a variant of the darkness in 316.

sentences.t:
Ἰδομενεὺς δ’ Ἐρύμαντα κατὰ στόμα νηλέϊ χαλκῷ
νύξε·
sentences.l:
And Idomeneus Erymas in the mouth with pitiless bronze
stabbed;
sentences.i: Idomeneus stabbed Erymas in the mouth with the pitiless bronze;
sentences.n: Ἐρύμας is Erymas; the Greek accusative is Ἐρύμαντα. κατὰ στόμα is ‘in the mouth’ and νηλέϊ χαλκῷ ‘with pitiless bronze’, the stock phrase for a spear-point. νύξε is ‘stabbed’ (the aorist of νύσσω); the object and the place come before it, so the verb waits at the start of the next line.

sentences.t:
τὸ δ’ ἀντικρὺ δόρυ χάλκεον ἐξεπέρησε
νέρθεν ὑπ’ ἐγκεφάλοιο, κέασσε δ’ ἄρ’ ὀστέα λευκά·
sentences.l:
and straight through the bronze spear passed out,
from below, beneath the brain, and split the white bones;
sentences.i: and the bronze spear passed clean through and out beneath the brain, and split the white bones;
sentences.n: τὸ δόρυ χάλκεον is ‘the bronze spear’, with τό the article. ἐξεπέρησε is the aorist of ἐκπεράω ‘pass right through and out’. νέρθεν is ‘from below’, and ὑπ’ ἐγκεφάλοιο is ‘beneath the brain’, with the epic genitive ending -οιο. κέασσε is the aorist of κεάζω ‘split’, and ὀστέα λευκά are ‘white bones’; the spear has gone in at the mouth and up under the brain.

sentences.t:
ἐκ δ’ ἐτίναχθεν ὀδόντες, ἐνέπλησθεν δέ οἱ ἄμφω
αἵματος ὀφθαλμοί·
sentences.l:
and out were shaken the teeth, and filled for him both
with blood the eyes;
sentences.i: his teeth were knocked out, and both his eyes filled with blood;
sentences.n: ἐκ … ἐτίναχθεν is ‘were shaken out’, the aorist passive of ἐκτινάσσω, the preverb ἐκ standing apart. ἐνέπλησθεν is ‘were filled’, the aorist passive of ἐμπίμπλημι, and the genitive αἵματος ‘with blood’ tells with what. οἱ is ‘his’ (‘for him’), and ἄμφω ὀφθαλμοί is ‘both eyes’.

sentences.t:
τὸ δ’ ἀνὰ στόμα καὶ κατὰ ῥῖνας
πρῆσε χανών·
sentences.l:
and it, up through the mouth and down through the nostrils,
he blew out, gaping;
sentences.i: and, gaping, he blew it out through his mouth and nostrils;
sentences.n: τό ‘it’ is the blood of the line before. ἀνὰ στόμα καὶ κατὰ ῥῖνας is ‘up through the mouth and down through the nostrils’ (ἀνά and κατά with the accusative of the place passed). πρῆσε is the aorist of πρήθω ‘blow, puff out’, and χανών, aorist participle of χάσκω, ‘gaping’.

sentences.t: θανάτου δὲ μέλαν νέφος ἀμφεκάλυψεν.
sentences.l: and the black cloud of death covered him about.
sentences.i: and the black cloud of death closed over him.
sentences.n: θανάτου μέλαν νέφος is ‘the black cloud of death’, an image the Odyssey uses in the same way (with θανάτοιο). ἀμφεκάλυψεν is ἀμφεκάλυψε, ‘covered about’, the aorist of ἀμφικαλύπτω.

sentences.t: οὗτοι ἄρ’ ἡγεμόνες Δαναῶν ἕλον ἄνδρα ἕκαστος.
sentences.l: These then, the leaders of the Danaans, took a man each.
sentences.i: These, then, were the leaders of the Danaans, and each of them killed a man.
sentences.n: The line closes the run of kills that opened at 306: οὗτοι ἄρ’ ἡγεμόνες ‘these then, the leaders’, ἕκαστος ‘each’. ἕλον ἄνδρα ‘took a man’ is ‘killed a man’, as at 306. A new paragraph begins here.

sentences.t:
ὡς δὲ λύκοι ἄρνεσσιν ἐπέχραον ἢ ἐρίφοισι
σίνται ὑπ’ ἐκ μήλων αἱρεύμενοι,
sentences.l:
And as wolves fall upon lambs or kids,
ravagers, taking them from under the flocks,
sentences.i: As wolves fall upon lambs or kids, ravagers that carry them off from the flock,
sentences.n: A simile for the Danaans among the Trojans, which line 356 answers with ὣς. ὡς δέ ‘and as’ starts it, and the aorist ἐπέχραον ‘fell upon’ (ἐπιχραύω, with the dative) is the aorist of a general truth and is put in the present, as in the other similes. ἄρνεσσιν ἢ ἐρίφοισι is ‘lambs or kids’. σίνται is the plural of σίντης ‘ravager’, a rare noun in apposition to λύκοι. ὑπ’ ἐκ μήλων is ‘out from under the flocks’ (μῆλα ‘flocks’), and αἱρεύμενοι ‘taking’ is the present participle of αἱρέω, here a middle form in -ευ-.

sentences.t:
αἵ τ’ ἐν ὄρεσσι
ποιμένος ἀφραδίῃσι διέτμαγεν·
sentences.l:
which on the mountains
through the follies of the shepherd have been split apart;
sentences.i: which have got separated on the mountains through the shepherd’s folly;
sentences.n: αἵ ‘which’ is feminine plural and takes up the lambs and kids. ποιμένος ἀφραδίῃσι is ‘through the shepherd’s follies’, the dative plural of ἀφραδίη, which the plain English gives as ‘folly’. διέτμαγεν is the aorist passive (-εν for -ησαν) of διατμήγω ‘cut apart’, put as a present perfect in English since the simile speaks in general. The verb is plural, the lambs and kids being the subject.

sentences.t:
οἳ δὲ ἰδόντες
αἶψα διαρπάζουσιν ἀνάλκιδα θυμὸν ἐχούσας·
sentences.l:
and they, having seen them,
at once tear them apart, having a heart without might;
sentences.i: and the wolves, seeing them, at once tear them apart, creatures whose heart has no might;
sentences.n: οἳ δέ ‘and they’ are the wolves, ἰδόντες ‘having seen’ (aorist participle of ὁράω). διαρπάζουσιν ‘tear apart’ is the present of διαρπάζω and αἶψα ‘at once’ an adverb. ἀνάλκιδα θυμὸν ἐχούσας is ‘having a heart without might’: ἄναλκις is ‘without might’ (ἀλκή ‘might’), here agreeing with θυμόν, and ἐχούσας is feminine, ‘the ones having’, picking out the lambs and kids.

sentences.t: ὣς Δαναοὶ Τρώεσσιν ἐπέχραον·
sentences.l: so the Danaans fell upon the Trojans;
sentences.i: so the Danaans fell upon the Trojans;
sentences.n: ὣς answers the ὡς of line 352, and now ἐπέχραον is a real past tense about the Danaans and the Trojans, not a general truth. Δαναοί are the Danaans.

sentences.t:
οἳ δὲ φόβοιο
δυσκελάδου μνήσαντο, λάθοντο δὲ θούριδος ἀλκῆς.
sentences.l:
and they of flight, ill-sounding,
remembered, and forgot impetuous might.
sentences.i: but they remembered flight, with its dismal din, and forgot their impetuous might.
sentences.n: οἳ δέ ‘and they’ are the Trojans. φόβοιο is ‘of flight’, φόβος in battle being the running that fear drives; δυσκελάδου, ‘ill-sounding’, is from δυσ- ‘ill’ and κέλαδος ‘din’, a rare adjective, and the plain English says ‘with its dismal din’. μνήσαντο is the aorist middle of μιμνήσκομαι ‘remember’ with the genitive, and λάθοντο is the aorist middle of λανθάνομαι ‘forget’ with the genitive θούριδος ἀλκῆς ‘impetuous might’, a stock phrase.

sentences.t:
Αἴας δ’ ὃ μέγας αἰὲν ἐφ’ Ἕκτορι χαλκοκορυστῇ
ἵετ’ ἀκοντίσσαι·
sentences.l:
And Ajax, the great one, always at Hector, bronze-armed,
was eager to cast;
sentences.i: But great Ajax was always eager to cast at Hector, armed in bronze;
sentences.n: Αἴας ὃ μέγας is ‘Ajax the great’, the son of Telamon, as against the lesser Ajax of line 330. Ἕκτορι χαλκοκορυστῇ is ‘at Hector, bronze-armed’, ἐπί with the dative saying whom he aims at; χαλκοκορυστής is ‘armed in bronze’ (κορύσσω ‘arm’). ἵετ’ is ἵετο, the imperfect middle of ἵημι, which with an infinitive means ‘be eager to’, and ἀκοντίσσαι is the aorist infinitive ‘to cast’. A new paragraph begins here.

sentences.t:
ὃ δὲ ἰδρείῃ πολέμοιο
ἀσπίδι ταυρείῃ κεκαλυμμένος εὐρέας ὤμους
σκέπτετ’ ὀϊστῶν τε ῥοῖζον καὶ δοῦπον ἀκόντων.
sentences.l:
but he, in knowledge of war,
covered as to his broad shoulders with a shield of bull’s hide,
watched for the whistling of arrows and the thud of javelins.
sentences.i: but Hector, with his knowledge of war, kept his broad shoulders covered with his shield of bull’s hide and watched for the whistle of arrows and the thud of javelins.
sentences.n: ὃ δέ ‘but he’ is Hector. ἰδρείῃ πολέμοιο is ‘by his knowledge of war’, ἰδρείη being skill that comes from knowing. κεκαλυμμένος is the perfect passive participle of καλύπτω, ‘covered’, with εὐρέας ὤμους ‘his broad shoulders’ as the accusative of the part covered, and the shield is ἀσπίδι ταυρείῃ, ‘a shield of bull’s hide’. σκέπτετ’ is σκέπτετο, ‘looked out for’. ῥοῖζον is the ‘whistling’ of a missile, δοῦπον the ‘thud’ (the noise of 325), and ὀϊστῶν and ἀκόντων are ‘arrows’ and ‘javelins’.

sentences.t: ἦ μὲν δὴ γίγνωσκε μάχης ἑτεραλκέα νίκην·
sentences.l: Truly he knew the victory in battle, other-strengthening;
sentences.i: He knew well that the victory in battle was turning the fight to the other side;
sentences.n: ἦ μὲν δή ‘truly indeed’ is emphatic. γίγνωσκε is ‘recognised, knew’. ἑτεραλκέα νίκην is ‘a victory that gives strength to the other side’, built on ἕτερος ‘other’ and ἀλκή ‘might’; the word is the one at 7.26, and the sense is that the day is going to the Achaeans, which the plain English spells out. μάχης is ‘of battle’, the genitive with νίκην.

sentences.t: ἀλλὰ καὶ ὧς ἀνέμιμνε, σάω δ’ ἐρίηρας ἑταίρους.
sentences.l: but even so he stayed, and was saving his trusty companions.
sentences.i: but even so he stood his ground and kept his trusty companions safe.
sentences.n: ἀλλὰ καὶ ὧς is ‘but even so’. ἀνέμιμνε is ‘stayed, waited’, the imperfect of ἀναμίμνω, and σάω is the third singular imperfect of σαόω ‘save’ (contracted from σάοε, with no augment), so the English has ‘kept safe’. ἐρίηρας ἑταίρους is ‘trusty companions’; the exact sense of ἐρίηρος is not fully known.

sentences.t:
ὡς δ’ ὅτ’ ἀπ’ Οὐλύμπου νέφος ἔρχεται οὐρανὸν εἴσω
αἰθέρος ἐκ δίης, ὅτε τε Ζεὺς λαίλαπα τείνῃ,
sentences.l:
And as when from Olympus a cloud goes into heaven
out of the heavenly aether, when Zeus stretches out a squall,
sentences.i: As when a cloud comes from Olympus into heaven, out of the heavenly aether, when Zeus spreads a squall,
sentences.n: A simile begins; ὣς in the next unit answers it. ὡς δ’ ὅτε is ‘as when’. οὐρανὸν εἴσω is ‘into heaven’, εἴσω the adverb ‘in, within’. αἰθέρος ἐκ δίης is ‘out of the heavenly aether’: αἰθήρ is the bright upper air, and δίης is the feminine genitive of δῖος ‘heavenly’. ὅτε τε … τείνῃ is ‘when he stretches’, a subjunctive with the particle τε of general statements; λαῖλαψ (λαίλαπα) is ‘squall’, and τείνω ‘stretch, spread’. A new paragraph begins here.

sentences.t:
ὣς τῶν ἐκ νηῶν γένετο ἰαχή τε φόβος τε,
οὐδὲ κατὰ μοῖραν πέραον πάλιν.
sentences.l:
so of those from the ships there arose a cry and flight,
and not according to what is fitting did they cross back.
sentences.i: so from the ships there arose from them a cry and flight, and they did not get back across as was fitting.
sentences.n: ὣς τῶν ‘so of them’ points to the Trojans being driven from the ships. ἰαχή τε φόβος τε is ‘a cry and flight’ (compare ἰαχή τε πόνος τε at 4.456). οὐδὲ κατὰ μοῖραν is ‘and not as is fitting’, the Odyssey’s phrase (3.331), meaning not in good order. πέραον is the imperfect of περάω ‘cross’, and πάλιν ‘back’; what they are crossing, the ditch, is named in line 369.

sentences.t:
Ἕκτορα δ’ ἵπποι
ἔκφερον ὠκύποδες σὺν τεύχεσι,
sentences.l:
and Hector the horses
bore out, swift-footed, with his armour,
sentences.i: and the swift-footed horses carried Hector out with his armour,
sentences.n: Ἕκτορα is the object, put first; ἵπποι ὠκύποδες ‘the swift-footed horses’ is the subject and ἔκφερον ‘bore out’ the imperfect of ἐκφέρω. ὠκύποδες is ὠκύς ‘swift’ with πούς ‘foot’. σὺν τεύχεσι ‘with his armour’ says Hector was carried off with all his gear, not stripped of it.

sentences.t:
λεῖπε δὲ λαὸν
Τρωϊκόν, οὓς ἀέκοντας ὀρυκτὴ τάφρος ἔρυκε.
sentences.l:
and he left the Trojan
people, whom, unwilling, the dug ditch held back.
sentences.i: and he left behind the Trojan army, which the dug ditch was holding back against its will.
sentences.n: The subject of λεῖπε is Hector (the verb is singular). λαὸν Τρωϊκόν is ‘the Trojan army’; Τρωϊκός is ‘Trojan’ and the diaeresis shows that the ι is a syllable of its own, so the word has three syllables. οὓς ἀέκοντας is ‘whom unwilling’, the relative with its predicate. ὀρυκτὴ τάφρος is ‘the dug ditch’, the trench the Achaeans dug to guard their ships (7.440), and ἔρυκε is ‘held back’, the imperfect of ἐρύκω.

sentences.t:
πολλοὶ δ’ ἐν τάφρῳ ἐρυσάρματες ὠκέες ἵπποι
ἄξαντ’ ἐν πρώτῳ ῥυμῷ λίπον ἅρματ’ ἀνάκτων,
sentences.l:
and many in the ditch chariot-drawing swift horses
having snapped, at the pole’s tip, left the chariots of their lords,
sentences.i: and in the ditch many swift, chariot-drawing horses snapped the pole at its tip and left the chariots of their lords behind,
sentences.n: ἐρυσάρματες ὠκέες ἵπποι is ‘swift, chariot-drawing horses’; ἐρυσάρματες is ἐρύω ‘draw’ with ἅρμα ‘chariot’. ἄξαντ’ is the aorist participle of ἄγνυμι ‘break’, the dual ἄξαντε with its ending elided (a plural in -ες could not be elided), each pair of horses having snapped its pole, and ἐν πρώτῳ ῥυμῷ ‘at the pole’s tip’ is the front end of the chariot-pole, to which the horses are yoked; the pole snapped and the horses went on, leaving ἅρματ’ ἀνάκτων ‘the chariots of their lords’ behind.

sentences.t:
Πάτροκλος δ’ ἕπετο σφεδανὸν Δαναοῖσι κελεύων
Τρωσὶ κακὰ φρονέων·
sentences.l:
and Patroclus followed furiously, bidding the Danaans on,
thinking evils for the Trojans;
sentences.i: and Patroclus followed furiously, calling on the Danaans, with evil in his mind for the Trojans;
sentences.n: Πάτροκλος is named for the first time in this part. σφεδανόν is ‘furiously’, an adverb, and ἕπετο is the imperfect of ἕπομαι ‘follow’. Δαναοῖσι κελεύων is ‘bidding the Danaans on’, κελεύω taking the dative here. Τρωσὶ κακὰ φρονέων is ‘thinking evils for the Trojans’, with κακά ‘evils’ the neuter plural object.

sentences.t:
οἳ δὲ ἰαχῇ τε φόβῳ τε
πάσας πλῆσαν ὁδούς, ἐπεὶ ἂρ τμάγεν·
sentences.l:
and they with cry and flight
filled all the roads, when they were split apart;
sentences.i: and with their cry and flight the Trojans filled all the roads, once they had been scattered;
sentences.n: οἳ δέ ‘and they’ are the Trojans. ἰαχῇ τε φόβῳ τε is ‘with cry and flight’ (366). πλῆσαν is ἔπλησαν, the aorist of πίμπλημι ‘fill’, and ἐπεὶ ἂρ τμάγεν ‘when they were split apart’ is the aorist passive of τμήγω (the same verb as διέτμαγεν at 354, third plural in -εν for -ησαν).

sentences.t:
ὕψι δ’ ἀέλλη
σκίδναθ’ ὑπὸ νεφέων,
sentences.l:
and high up the blast
was spreading itself beneath the clouds,
sentences.i: and high up beneath the clouds the storm spread out,
sentences.n: ἀέλλη is a blast of wind, ‘storm’ in the plain English; here it is understood as the whirl of dust the flight raises, which the Greek does not say. σκίδναθ’ is σκίδνατο, the imperfect middle of σκίδνημι ‘scatter’, here ‘spread itself out’. ὑπὸ νεφέων is ‘beneath the clouds’, νεφέων being the epic genitive plural.

sentences.t:
τανύοντο δὲ μώνυχες ἵπποι
ἄψορρον προτὶ ἄστυ νεῶν ἄπο καὶ κλισιάων.
sentences.l:
and the solid-hoofed horses stretched themselves out
back toward the city, away from the ships and the huts.
sentences.i: and the solid-hoofed horses strained back toward the city, away from the ships and the huts.
sentences.n: τανύοντο is the imperfect middle of τανύω ‘stretch’, ‘stretched themselves out’ in a hard run. μώνυχες ἵπποι is ‘solid-hoofed horses’, the stock phrase for horses with a whole hoof, and ἄψορρον is an adverb, ‘back’. νεῶν ἄπο καὶ κλισιάων is ‘away from the ships and the huts’, with ἄπο standing after its nouns and κλισιάων the epic genitive plural of κλισίη.

sentences.t:
Πάτροκλος δ’ ᾗ πλεῖστον ὀρινόμενον ἴδε λαόν,
τῇ ῥ’ ἔχ’ ὁμοκλήσας·
sentences.l:
And Patroclus, where he saw the army most stirred up,
there held on, having shouted;
sentences.i: And where Patroclus saw the army most stirred up, he held his course, shouting;
sentences.n: ᾗ … τῇ ῥ’ is ‘where … there’, adverbs of place. πλεῖστον ὀρινόμενον … λαόν is ‘the army most stirred up’, with ὀρινόμενον the present passive participle of ὀρίνω ‘stir up’; the army is the Trojan one. ἔχ’ is ἔχε, the imperfect of ἔχω, ‘held on’ without an object, probably his horses, and ὁμοκλήσας ‘having shouted’ is the aorist participle of ὁμοκλάω, again without a stated object.

sentences.t:
ὑπὸ δ’ ἄξοσι φῶτες ἔπιπτον
πρηνέες ἐξ ὀχέων, δίφροι δ’ ἀνακυμβαλίαζον.
sentences.l:
and beneath the axles men were falling
headlong from the chariots, and the chariots were tumbling over.
sentences.i: and men fell face down from their chariots beneath the axles, and the chariots went tumbling over.
sentences.n: ὑπὸ δ’ ἄξοσι is ‘beneath the axles’, where the men land; ἄξοσι is the dative plural of ἄξων. φῶτες ‘men’ is the subject of ἔπιπτον ‘were falling’, and πρηνέες is ‘headlong’ in the literal line, ‘face down’ in the plain English. ὀχέων ‘chariots’ and δίφροι ‘chariots’ are two words with one English; δίφρος is the chariot body. ἀνακυμβαλίαζον is a rare verb found only here, and ‘were tumbling over’ is the sense usually taken.

sentences.t:
ἀντικρὺ δ’ ἄρα τάφρον ὑπέρθορον ὠκέες ἵπποι
ἄμβροτοι, οὓς Πηλῆϊ θεοὶ δόσαν ἀγλαὰ δῶρα,
sentences.l:
and straight over the ditch leapt the swift horses,
deathless, which to Peleus the gods gave, splendid gifts,
sentences.i: and straight over the ditch leapt the swift, deathless horses, which the gods gave to Peleus as splendid gifts,
sentences.n: These are Achilles’ own horses, Xanthus and Balius, who are named at 16.149. ἀντικρύ is ‘straight’, and ὑπέρθορον is the aorist of ὑπερθρῴσκω ‘leap over’. ὠκέες ἵπποι is ‘swift horses’ and ἄμβροτοι ‘deathless’, the stock epithets. οὓς Πηλῆϊ θεοὶ δόσαν is ‘which the gods gave to Peleus’ (δόσαν for ἔδοσαν), and ἀγλαὰ δῶρα ‘splendid gifts’ is in apposition to οὕς. Πηλῆϊ is the dative of Πηλεύς.

sentences.t: πρόσσω ἱέμενοι, ἐπὶ δ’ Ἕκτορι κέκλετο θυμός·
sentences.l: eager onward, and upon Hector his heart called;
sentences.i: pressing eagerly on, and his heart urged him on toward Hector;
sentences.n: ἱέμενοι is ‘eager’, the present participle of ἵεμαι, and πρόσσω ‘onward’ an adverb. ἐπὶ … κέκλετο is the tmesis of ἐπικέκλετο, ‘called on’ (κέκλετο is the aorist of κέλομαι with no augment), and the subject is Patroclus’ θυμός ‘heart’, so Patroclus is urged on against Hector; the Greek has no word for ‘him’.

sentences.t: ἵετο γὰρ βαλέειν· τὸν δ’ ἔκφερον ὠκέες ἵπποι.
sentences.l: for he was eager to strike; but him the swift horses bore out.
sentences.i: for he longed to strike him; but the swift horses were carrying Hector off.
sentences.n: ἵετο γάρ ‘for he was eager’ gives the reason for the heart’s urging. βαλέειν is the aorist infinitive of βάλλω ‘strike’, with no object stated. τὸν δ’ ἔκφερον is ‘but him they bore out’, the same verb as at 368; τόν is Hector.

sentences.t:
ὡς δ’ ὑπὸ λαίλαπι πᾶσα κελαινὴ βέβριθε χθὼν
ἤματ’ ὀπωρινῷ, ὅτε λαβρότατον χέει ὕδωρ
Ζεύς,
sentences.l:
And as beneath a squall all the dark earth is weighed down
on a late-summer day, when most violent water pours
Zeus,
sentences.i: And as under a squall the whole dark earth is weighed down on a late-summer day, when Zeus pours out water most violently,
sentences.n: A second simile for the same flight. ὡς δ’ is ‘and as’; ὑπὸ λαίλαπι is ‘under a squall’, βέβριθε is the perfect of βρίθω ‘be heavy’, here ‘is weighed down’ by the storm, and κελαινή ‘dark’ goes with χθών ‘earth’. ἤματ’ ὀπωρινῷ is ‘on a late-summer day’, the season of storms after harvest. λαβρότατον is the superlative of λάβρος ‘violent’, with ὕδωρ ‘water’, and the plain English puts it as an adverb; Ζεύς is at the end of the unit and is the subject of χέει ‘pours’.

sentences.t: ὅτε δή ῥ’ ἄνδρεσσι κοτεσσάμενος χαλεπήνῃ,
sentences.l: when indeed, bearing a grudge against men, he grows harsh,
sentences.i: when, bearing a grudge against men, he grows angry,
sentences.n: ὅτε δή ῥ’ is ‘when indeed’, and the subjunctive χαλεπήνῃ ‘grows harsh’ (χαλεπαίνω) is a general statement. κοτεσσάμενος is the aorist participle of κοτέω ‘bear a grudge’, with ἄνδρεσσι, the epic dative plural of ἀνήρ, ‘against men’. The men and their fault are named in the next lines.

sentences.t: οἳ βίῃ εἰν ἀγορῇ σκολιὰς κρίνωσι θέμιστας,
sentences.l: who by force in the assembly decide crooked rules of right,
sentences.i: men who by force in the assembly pass crooked judgments,
sentences.n: οἳ … κρίνωσι ‘who decide’ is a subjunctive of general statement (κρίνω ‘judge, decide’). βίῃ is ‘by force’ and εἰν ἀγορῇ ‘in the assembly’ (εἰν for ἐν). σκολιάς ‘crooked’ goes with θέμιστας, the plural of θέμις ‘rule of right’; the judgments of a court are meant, which is what the plain English says.

sentences.t: ἐκ δὲ δίκην ἐλάσωσι θεῶν ὄπιν οὐκ ἀλέγοντες·
sentences.l: and drive justice out, not heeding the retribution of the gods;
sentences.i: and drive justice out, with no heed for the gods’ retribution;
sentences.n: ἐκ … ἐλάσωσι is ‘drive out’ with the preverb apart, and δίκην ‘justice’ is its object; ἐλάσωσι is the aorist subjunctive of ἐλαύνω. θεῶν ὄπιν is ‘the retribution of the gods’; ὄπις is a rare noun whose sense is not certain, and ‘retribution’ is the Odyssey’s rendering. οὐκ ἀλέγοντες is ‘not heeding’, the participle of ἀλέγω.

sentences.t: τῶν δέ τε πάντες μὲν ποταμοὶ πλήθουσι ῥέοντες,
sentences.l: and of them all the rivers are full, flowing,
sentences.i: and because of such men all the rivers run full,
sentences.n: τῶν is the plural genitive ‘of them’ and looks back to the men of 387–388 who pass crooked judgments: the rivers run full on their account. The plain English says ‘because of such men’. πάντες … ποταμοὶ πλήθουσι ῥέοντες is ‘all the rivers are full, flowing’; πλήθουσι is the present of πλήθω ‘be full’, and ῥέοντες the participle of ῥέω ‘flow’. δέ τε … is the particle pair of a general statement.

sentences.t: πολλὰς δὲ κλιτῦς τότ’ ἀποτμήγουσι χαράδραι,
sentences.l: and many slopes then the ravines cut away,
sentences.i: and then the ravines cut away many hillsides,
sentences.n: κλιτῦς is the accusative plural of κλιτύς ‘slope’, and ἀποτμήγουσι is the present of ἀποτμήγω ‘cut away’; χαράδραι are the ‘ravines’ cut by the torrents. τότ’ ‘then’ is the time of the storm.

sentences.t:
ἐς δ’ ἅλα πορφυρέην μεγάλα στενάχουσι ῥέουσαι
ἐξ ὀρέων ἐπικάρ,
sentences.l:
and into the purple sea they groan greatly as they flow
from the mountains, head first,
sentences.i: and as they flow they groan loudly into the purple sea, plunging down from the mountains,
sentences.n: The subject of στενάχουσι is the ravines (χαράδραι) of the line before, as the feminine participle ῥέουσαι shows; the rivers (masculine) are not the subject. ἐς … ἅλα πορφυρέην is ‘into the purple sea’; the colour word is the same πορφύρεος as in 334, here for the sea. μεγάλα is ‘greatly’, the neuter plural as an adverb, and στενάχουσι ‘groan’ is a verb for loud sound. ῥέουσαι is the feminine participle ‘flowing’. ἐπικάρ is an adverb built on the root of κάρη ‘head’, ‘head first’; the exact sense is not certain, and the plain English has ‘plunging’.

sentences.t: μινύθει δέ τε ἔργ’ ἀνθρώπων·
sentences.l: and the works of men grow less;
sentences.i: and the works of men dwindle away;
sentences.n: μινύθει is the present of μινύθω, here intransitive, ‘grow less, dwindle’; ἔργ’ ἀνθρώπων is ‘the works of men’ (probably fields and what they have built), and δέ τε is again the particle pair of a general statement. The torrent has carried them away.

sentences.t: ὣς ἵπποι Τρῳαὶ μεγάλα στενάχοντο θέουσαι.
sentences.l: so the Trojan mares greatly groaned, running.
sentences.i: so the Trojan mares groaned loudly as they ran.
sentences.n: ὣς answers the simile that began at 384. ἵπποι Τρῳαί has a feminine adjective, so the horses are mares; Τρῳαί is the feminine form of ‘Trojan’. μεγάλα στενάχοντο is ‘groaned greatly’, the imperfect of στενάχομαι, and θέουσαι is the feminine present participle of θέω ‘run’. The verb for groaning is the one used of the torrents in 391.
